etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English mouth, from Old English mūþ, from Proto-West Germanic *munþ, from Proto-Germanic *munþaz (“mouth”), from Proto-Indo-European *ment- (“to chew; jaw, mouth”). Cognate with Scots mooth (“mouth”), North Frisian müd, müth, müss (“mouth”), West Frisian mûn (“mouth”), Dutch mond (“mouth”), muide (“river mouth”) and mui (“riptide”), German Mund (“mouth”), Swedish mun (“mouth”), Norwegian munn (“mouth”), Danish mund (“mouth”), Faroese muður, munnur (“mouth”), Icelandic munnur (“mouth”), Gothic 𐌼𐌿𐌽𐌸𐍃 (munþs, “mouth”), Latin mentum (“chin”) and mandō (“to chew”), Ancient Greek μάσταξ (mástax, “jaws, mouth”) and μασάομαι (masáomai, “to chew”), Albanian mjekër (“chin, beard”), Welsh mant (“jawbone”), Hittite [script needed] (mēni, “chin”). The verb is from Middle English mouthen, from the noun.

definitions.definition: (anatomy) The opening of a creature through which food is ingested.

quote.citation: 1913, Joseph C[rosby] Lincoln, chapter VII, in Mr. Pratt’s Patients, New York, N.Y., London: D[aniel] Appleton and Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: I made a speaking trumpet of my hands and commenced to whoop “Ahoy!” and “Hello!” at the top of my lungs.  […]  The Colonel woke up, and, after asking what in brimstone was the matter, opened his mouth and roared “Hi!” and “Hello!” like the bull of Bashan.

definitions.definition: The end of a river out of which water flows into a sea or other large body of water; or the end of a tributary out of which water flows into a larger river.
An outlet, aperture or orifice.

quote.citation: 1764, Horace Walpole, The Castle of Otranto:
quote.text: But come, Lady, we are too near the mouth of the cavern; let us seek its inmost recesses.

quote.citation: 1963, Margery Allingham, chapter 1, in The China Governess: A Mystery, London: Chatto & Windus, →OCLC:
quote.text: ‘It was called the wickedest street in London and the entrance was just here. I imagine the mouth of the road lay between this lamp standard and the second from the next down there.’

quote.citation: 2020 August 26, Tim Dunn, “Great railway bores of our time!”, in Rail, page 42:
quote.text: But why give a tunnel mouth any decoration whatsoever?

definitions.definition: (slang) A loud or overly talkative person.
(slang) A gossip.

quote.citation: 2012, Stuart Carolan, 40:45 from the start, in Love/Hate, season 3, episode 3, spoken by Tommy Daly (Killian Scott):
quote.text: Siobhán, you know Donna's a mouth.

definitions.definition: (saddlery) The crosspiece of a bridle bit, which enters the mouth of an animal.
(obsolete) A principal speaker; one who utters the common opinion; a mouthpiece.

quote.citation: 1712 June 23 (Gregorian calendar), [Joseph Addison; Richard Steele et al.], “THURSDAY, June 12, 1712”, in The Spectator, number 403; republished in Alexander Chalmers, editor, The Spectator; a New Edition, […], volume IV, New York, N.Y.: D[aniel] Appleton & Company, 1853, →OCLC:
quote.text: Every coffeehouse has some particular statesman belonging to it, who is the mouth of the street where he lives.The spelling has been modernized.

definitions.definition: (obsolete) Speech; language; testimony.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Matthew 18:16:
quote.text: that in the mouth of two or three witnesses every word may be established

definitions.definition: (obsolete) A wry face; a grimace; a mow.

quote.citation: c. 1595–1596 (date written), William Shakespeare, “A Midsommer Nights Dreame”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies: Published According to the True Originall Copies (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act III, scene ii]:
quote.text: Counterfeit sad looks, / Make mouths upon me when I turn my back.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To speak; to utter.

quote.citation: 1826, Julius Hare, Guesses at Truth by Two Brothers:
quote.text: mouthing big phrases

definitions.definition: (transitive) To represent (words or sounds) by making the actions of speech, but silently, without producing sound; to frame.

quote.citation: 2010, Jan Faull, Jennifer McLean Oliver, Amazing Minds:
quote.text: One was of a face repeatedly mouthing the vowel sound eee, the other was of a face repeatedly mouthing the vowel sound ahhh.

quote.citation: 2016, Wayne Morris, Theology without Words: Theology in the Deaf Community:
quote.text: It should be explained that lip patterns are generally not the same as patterns which would be made by 'mouthing' words.

quote.citation: 2020, Wanitta Praks, Maid to the Mafia:
quote.text: "So very hot,” I mouthed at myself in the mirror.

definitions.definition: (transitive, intransitive) To move the mouth, with or without sound; to form (air or words) with the mouth, with or without sound.

quote.citation: 1886, James Hogg, Polmood series, page 51:
quote.text: But words are nothing to the misbelieving -- mere air mouthed into a sound.

quote.citation: 1987, Peter H. Wolff, The Development of Behavioral States and the Expression of Emotions in Early Infancy, page 15:
quote.text: There was also a close temporal contiguity between "smiling" or other "emotional" grimaces and mouthing and tonguing movements, so that it was often difficult to distinguish between mouthing and smiling.

definitions.definition: (transitive, intransitive) To utter with a voice that is overly loud or swelling.

quote.citation: 1846, Erasmus Darwin North, Practical Speaking: As Taught in Yale College, page 123:
quote.text: Those who endeavor to become eloquent by mere imitation of some celebrated model—an actor for instance—often attempt to gain this quality by altering their voice in an unnatural manner. Such a process never produces any thing but mouthing.

quote.citation: 1902, George Andrew Lewis, The Practical treatment of stammering and stuttering, page 195:
quote.text: This view of voice cultivation excludes all mouthing and ranting which have been thought to be necessary incidents of voice culture.

definitions.definition: To exit at a mouth (such as a river mouth)

quote.citation: 1906, Philosophical Magazine, page 96:
quote.text: In this part of the address the position of the principal hanging-valleys was indicated , and it was pointed out that there were two sets, namely those which mouthed into valleys that had been deepened in softer rocks, and those which  mouthed into portions of main valleys that had been deepened along shatter-bolts.

quote.citation: 1999, T. Walter Middleton, Qualla: Home of the Middle Cherokee Settlement, page 39:
quote.text: Suddenly an avalanche of stones turned loose right down a ravine and mouthed out on the road, stones large enough to knock a horse down, or larger, and a plenty of them to do a fair job on a large group.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To pick up or handle with the lips or mouth, but not chew or swallow.

quote.text: His manner of feeding was curious, any fish he was provided with not being snapped up immediately, but played with and mouthed all over for a quarter of an hour or more, when it suddenly disappeared as if by magic.

quote.citation: 1920, James Willard Schultz, The Dreadful River Cave: Chief Black Elk's Story, page 50:

quote.citation: 1973, Thomas Pynchon, Gravity's Rainbow:
quote.text: Everyone is kind of aroused, Thanatz is sitting up on the bar having his own as yet unsheathed penis mouthed by one of the white-gloved Wends.

quote.citation: 1999, Laura Tice Lage, Sagebrush Homesteads, page 257:
quote.text: She found foamy saliva where the coyote had mouthed over the dogs, but no place showed any bite.

definitions.definition: To take into the mouth; to seize or grind with the mouth or teeth; to chew; to devour.

quote.citation: 1938, Jack Common, Seven Shifts, page 62:
quote.text: Sometimes I ate food that the rats had already mouthed over; picking away the edges where they had been eating and using the remainder; not with any good grace, not without qualms; but because I had nothing else to eat.

quote.citation: 1998, Marvin K. Rubin, Word of Mouth: A Manhattan Dentist Tells All-- (well, Almost), page 77:
quote.text: Each contained a long, wide, solid oak table around which all who could find a space the width of his body would mouth his brown-bag grub from home.

definitions.definition: To form or cleanse with the mouth; to lick, as a bear licks her cub.

quote.text: They were sucking off whatever adhered to the floating stems and leaves of the plants. They went from plant to plant and mouthed over each branch from base to tip until the whole plant had been gone over.

quote.citation: 1937, Aquarium Journal - Volume 10, Issue 5, page 7:
quote.text: Meanwhile she, and the male, mouthed over the inner surface of pot until it was as clean as could be.

quote.citation: 1965, The Aquarist and Pondkeeper - Volumes 30-31, page 182:

quote.citation: 1970, Christine Weston, The Hoopoe, page 6:
quote.text: Small slobs of things, wet and sticky, which Peggy herself distastefully mouthed out from her cavity, biting the cord which bound them to her, swallowing it, then licking the puppies clean one by one.

definitions.definition: To carry in the mouth.

definitions.definition: To form a mouth or opening in.

definitions.definition: (sheep husbandry) To examine the teeth of.

quote.text: Either at the shipping point or as they leave the summer range, the older ewes are “mouthed out.” That is, their mouths are examined to see if their teeth are good for another year.

While there is no doubt that the practice of “mouthing" ewes is founded on experience, the traditional standards may require modification since the adoption almost exclusively of grassland farming, particularly in the North Island.
